title: Saturnalia, roles reversed
hook: the Roman midwinter festival turned roles upside down; Seneca stayed sober and practiced poverty (Letters 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the autumn equinox, and Seneca laughing at his own old trees. Your line was the turning. Did you catch the dusk, and one thing the season gave? Day six hundred seventy-two, the end of a week.

Rome, mid-December. The streets are loud. People have swapped their formal togas for loose, bright dinner clothes. Shops are selling little clay figures and wax candles to give as presents. Gambling, usually frowned on, is allowed in public. In some households, ancient writers tell us, the strangest thing of all: for the feast, the enslaved people of the house are served, or sit at table with the family, and the masters wait on them. It's the Saturnalia, the festival of the god Saturn. And Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, has some thoughts about how to spend it.
screen: `ROME, MID-DECEMBER.` → `CANDLES, CLAY FIGURES, DICE.` → `THE MASTERS SERVE.`

segments.voice: First, the festival. The Saturnalia began on December seventeenth and grew over time to several days. Romans remembered Saturn's reign as a golden age, before rich and poor, when everyone was equal. For a few days, the festival played at that: freedom of speech, gifts, and roles turned upside down. It was a game, and the next week everything went back. Rome was a slave society, and we should say that plainly. But the game itself admitted something: the order of things wasn't the only possible one. Second, Seneca's letter. It's December, he writes, and the whole city is sweating with celebration. Should we join in, or stay apart? His answer is balanced: don't make a show of refusing, but don't lose yourself. Keep a sober head while others are drunk. Third, his surprising suggestion. While everyone feasts, he says, set aside a few days to live on the plainest, cheapest food and in rough clothing, and ask yourself: is this what I was afraid of? Rich people, he says, sometimes did this for fun; he means it as training, so that poverty, if it ever came, would hold no terror. Fourth, the reversal that lasts. Seneca wrote another letter arguing that the people who serve us are human beings like us, born of the same seed, under the same sky. Saturnalia flipped roles for a day. A Stoic tries to keep a little of that all year: seeing the person who brings your coffee, cleans the office, delivers the box, as fully a person, and acting like it. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: both ways. Equal light. Honest review. Long light, still passing. In season. The turning. Roles reversed.
screen: `SATURN'S GOLDEN AGE, PLAYED FOR DAYS.` · `SOBER WHILE THE CITY CELEBRATES.` · `PLAIN FOOD: IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?` · `THE PEOPLE WHO SERVE US ARE PEOPLE.` · then, large: `ROLES REVERSED.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who serve you in an ordinary week. The person at the counter. The driver. The cleaner. The teacher. Someone at home who does more than their share. Picture one of them clearly, their face, their voice. Imagine, just for a moment, that the roles were reversed and you were doing their work for them. How would you want to be treated? Then choose one small thing you could give them: a real thank-you, a tip, a kindness. The bell holds the time.
Saturnalia: the Roman midwinter festival when roles were reversed, and for Seneca a time to stay sober, practice simplicity, and remember who serves us. Today's word.
Your line: roles reversed. Give something today, even small, to someone who usually serves you, and look them in the eye when you do. Day six hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca mark busy festive seasons by keeping a few plain days, and by giving thanks or gifts to the people who serve them through the year.

fork.setup: you're Lucilius, and the whole city is feasting for the Saturnalia. what does Seneca advise?
options: join in, but keep a sober head
fork.reveal: Letter 18: don't make yourself conspicuous by refusing, but don't lose yourself either; and try a few plain days.

trapdoor: what you thought: Saturnalia was just an ancient Roman party.
what it means: it reversed roles for a few days, recalling a golden age of equality; Seneca used it for sobriety and simplicity.

what a scholar hears: Letters 18 opens in December with the city in a sweat; Letters 47 argues that slaves are human beings born of the same seed; Macrobius describes masters serving slaves at the feast.

notes: Letters 18 paraphrased (December, city in a sweat; should we join? be like the crowd outwardly but not in spirit; set aside days of scanty fare and coarse dress, asking 'Is this the condition that I feared?'). Confirm.
Letters 47: slaves as human beings 'sprung from the same stock, smiled upon by the same skies'. Paraphrased. Confirm.

Saturnalia details (Dec 17; extended to several days; sigillaria figurines and wax candles; gambling allowed; synthesis dinner clothes; masters serving slaves) from Macrobius and others. Practices varied by household and era; confirm.
Slavery named plainly as part of Roman society.
'Io Saturnalia' as the festive cry: confirm.
Reviewer edit: hook softened from 'in many households' to 'in some households, ancient writers tell us'; how widely masters actually served slaves is uncertain and sources are literary.

10% audit (year 2): cut the filler closing line of the week look-back ('a week of the calendar's markers, each one a small door into the same porch'); the carries list (666–672) checked against the files.
